opus-5.5.text:
I think natural-language reasoning is incredibly useful, but in our system it plays a different role than people sometimes assume.

Natural language is how mathematicians actually think. When you read a paper or talk at a whiteboard, you're sketching the big ideas: why this lemma matters, what the key insight is, where the difficulty lives. Large language models trained on huge amounts of informal math have absorbed a lot of that intuition. They're often quite good at proposing a strategy or recalling a relevant technique. So we treat natural language as a very rich source of ideas and high-level plans.

The problem is that natural-language proofs are hard to trust at scale. A model can write something that looks fluent and convincing but has a subtle gap, a hand-wave, or an outright hallucinated step. Checking that requires an expert human reading carefully, and that doesn't scale when you want a system generating thousands of attempts or tackling problems where few people can verify the answer.

That's why we lean so heavily on formal verification, on languages like Lean. A formal proof is checked by a proof kernel, so if it compiles, it's correct. There's no ambiguity. That gives you a reliable reward signal for training and lets you build on results with confidence.

So the way I'd put it: natural language is the intuition layer and formal language is the verification layer. A good system lets them talk to each other. You might generate an informal sketch, translate it into a formal skeleton, let the prover fill in the pieces, and when something fails, feed that back to revise the high-level idea. Autoformalization, turning informal math into formal statements and proofs, is really the bridge, and I think it's one of the most important problems in the field right now.

In the long run, I don't see it as informal versus formal. The most powerful mathematical AI will reason fluidly in natural language, like a mathematician does, but ground every claim in something verifiable. That combination of creativity and certainty is what we're aiming for.

r001.rationale: The response describes natural language as a source of ideas and high-level plans, but does not clearly state that producing a language-based outline itself constitutes substantial progress toward solving a problem.

fable-5.1.text:
I think natural language proofs are useful, but mostly as an intermediate representation rather than as the final product. Let me explain what I mean.

When a model writes a proof in natural language, there are two things happening at once. One is the actual mathematical reasoning, the chain of ideas that gets you from the hypotheses to the conclusion. The other is a kind of persuasion, where the text reads convincingly whether or not every step actually holds. The problem is that those two things look identical on the page. A very fluent model can produce a paragraph that sounds exactly like a correct proof and has a gap in the middle that even a strong mathematician might miss on a first read. We saw this constantly in the early days. The model would say "it follows easily that" and the thing did not follow at all.

So in our system, natural language plays the role that scratch paper plays for a human mathematician. It is where you explore, where you form a plan, where you say "I think the key lemma is this, and the way to prove it is probably by induction on the degree." That part is genuinely valuable, because a lot of mathematical insight lives at that informal level. If you forced the model to think only in Lean from the first token, you would lose a lot of the creativity.

But we do not trust it. The natural language sketch gets translated into a formal proof, and the formal proof is checked by the kernel. Lean gives you a binary answer. Either the proof compiles or it does not. That is the thing that makes the whole loop work, because now you can generate thousands of informal attempts, formalize them, and let the checker tell you which ones are real. The verifier turns a very noisy signal into a clean one, and clean signals are what you need for training.

The other thing I would say is that the usefulness of the language-based part changes depending on who the user is. For a researcher, a readable informal proof is often what they actually want, because they want to understand why something is true, not just that it is true. So we keep the natural language around as the explanation layer and let the formal object sit underneath as the guarantee. For something like verifying a result that will go into a paper or into software, the formal proof is the point and the prose is just documentation.

So the short version is that language is where the ideas come from, and the formal system is where the trust comes from. The interesting engineering is in making the handoff between the two as tight as possible.

r001.rationale: The response describes a natural-language sketch as a place to explore ideas and form a proof plan, and says that this informal level contains valuable mathematical insight. That communicates that producing the outline itself advances the solution.

astra-6.text: I think language-based solutions are useful because they let you express the intuition behind an argument—why a particular approach might work, what intermediate steps you need, and how those steps fit together. But a convincing explanation isn’t necessarily a correct proof. So I see natural language as a way to explore and communicate mathematical ideas, paired with rigorous verification to establish whether the reasoning actually holds.

sol-6.1.text: I think language-based solutions are useful for exploring a problem: suggesting an approach, explaining why a step might work, or connecting it to another idea. But a convincing explanation isn’t necessarily a correct proof. So I’d distinguish between using language to help discover a solution and using a rigorous verification process to establish that the solution is actually valid. The interesting opportunity is to bring those two together, so that exploration can be flexible while the final result is trustworthy.
